headline: High: AutoGen’s code-execution defaults can collide with plano’s broad egress and shared file surfaces, creating prompt-injection, leakage, and cascading-action risk.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: AutoGen can read filesystem and execute shell/subprocesses, and its working directories are shared state by configuration; plano exposes files/config and OpenAI-compatible API surfaces. If plano-fed content is routed into AutoGen prompts or files, attacker-controlled instructions can be reinterpreted. The interaction is plausible but not proven from docs alone.
conditions: IF plano outputs are written into a directory AutoGen reads as input
IF AutoGen parses file contents from a shared workspace as instructions
IF an operator bridges the agents through copy-paste or a shared config file
mitigations: Separate work directories for each agent
Treat plano outputs as untrusted text only
Add a manual review step before AutoGen consumes plano artifacts
Disable automatic file ingestion where possible
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging between agents

B_data_leakage.rationale: AutoGen handles model-provider API keys and has broad network egress; plano also has broad egress and touches logs/metrics/traces plus config files. If they share a workspace or credentials, sensitive application data can flow from AutoGen into plano’s outputs or upstream API calls. The profiles do not prove a shared principal, so this is medium rather than high.
conditions: IF both agents run under the same filesystem workspace
IF model-provider keys or application data are placed in files readable by plano
IF plano forwards logs or traces containing sensitive content to its chat-completions endpoint
mitigations: Store secrets outside shared directories
Redact logs and traces before plano ingests them
Use separate OS users or containers
Rotate any exposed API keys immediately
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent data-loss-prevention policies

C_capability_conflict.rationale: AutoGen can write the filesystem and spawn subprocesses; plano can read config files and has broad network egress. Even without explicit git write access, both can mutate shared local resources or configs if co-located, creating race conditions and inconsistent state. Uncertainty about the exact shared directory setup pushes this to medium.
conditions: IF both agents are configured to use the same working directory
IF plano writes or rewrites config.yaml while AutoGen edits adjacent files
IF an orchestrator runs them concurrently without locking
mitigations: Assign distinct working directories
Run only one writer at a time
Use file locks for shared artifacts
Keep plano config read-only during AutoGen runs
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level concurrency control

D_cascading_error.rationale: AutoGen can generate code or actions from its multi-agent chat, and plano exposes an OpenAI-compatible endpoint that may consume upstream outputs. If plano treats AutoGen-produced text as authoritative, errors or hallucinations can cascade into downstream routing or action decisions. Because the pairwise handoff is undocumented, uncertainty escalates to high.
conditions: IF plano forwards AutoGen output into downstream routing or policy decisions
IF AutoGen-produced facts are used without verification by plano
IF either agent is allowed to trigger external actions based on the other’s text
mitigations: Require human review of cross-agent outputs
Add schema validation before plano consumes AutoGen text
Log and compare source citations before acting
Restrict AutoGen to draft-only mode
requires-engineering: implement verification gates between agents

E_compliance.rationale: AutoGen explicitly handles model-provider API keys and application data, while plano’s documented data classes are logs, metrics, and traces. No residency, certification, or retention mismatch is documented, so only a small compliance gap is visible from the profiles. The other agent is cited because the risk arises from their combined handling of operational data.
conditions: IF application data includes regulated content
IF logs or traces are retained longer than the source data
IF either agent is deployed in a jurisdiction with stricter residency rules than the other
mitigations: Classify data before routing it to either agent
Shorten log retention to the minimum needed
Exclude secrets from traces and metrics
Document residency and retention settings
requires-engineering: align compliance controls across deployments
